name: Colonial Buff
lede: Colonial Buff is a pale orange-yellow traced furthest back of any color, to Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's Nomenclature of Colours, and later repeated by Ridgway, Maerz and Paul, and the ISCC-NBS.

sections.title: Four books, one swatch
sections.body:
Our library's earliest source for this name is Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, no. 71 among the yellows, from an aged swatch dated 1821 [1]. Ridgway's 1912 standard places the same name on plate XXX, hue 21′′, tone d, and Maerz and Paul repeat it in 1930; the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 assigns it block 86, light yellow, 5.2 units from that block's centroid [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[ochre-yellow]], [[leghorn]] and [[baryta-yellow]], at 2.6, 
Werner ties the same swatch to three things from nature: the fur of a polar bear, oat straw, and the minerals schorlite and calamine, a reminder that one 1821 color served every one of his readers' purposes at once [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Colonial Buff covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 705 of them, about 3.0 per cent, as photographed [3]. It plays a highlight in 97 per cent of its appearances, almost never a shadow, and peaks in paintings from the 1840s [3]. It is most devotedly used by Johan Hendrik Weissenbruch, in 3 of his 12 works [3]. These are museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen color, not a pigment identification [3].
